Security Practices

September 24, 2026 · Version 2.7

Security and privacy are foundational design constraints for Remvoll, not afterthoughts. This document describes our practices, our threat model, and — in the interest of honesty — the limits of what a local-first product can guarantee.

1. Threat model

For a local-first iOS application the principal risks are: (a) another person with access to your unlocked iPhone; (b) compromise of the device itself; and (c) supply-chain compromise of third-party code, which here is nil because there is none. By storing no user data on servers and holding no credentials at all, Remvoll eliminates entire classes of risk that affect conventional cloud products: large-scale server breaches, credential-stuffing databases, insider access to user records, and misconfigured cloud storage. There is nothing centralized to breach and no password to steal.

2. Authentication

There is none, and that is the design. Remvoll has no accounts, no sign-up, no password, no recovery code and no session. It therefore stores no credential of any kind, which removes password reuse, credential stuffing, account enumeration, session hijacking and account-recovery social engineering from the threat model entirely rather than mitigating them.

Access to the app is governed by the lock on your iPhone. Entitlement to paid features is decided by a signed receipt Apple issues to the device, not by anything we could be tricked into granting.

3. Data protection

  • AES-256-GCM authenticated encryption for every record in Remvoll's encrypted store — settings, presets, sleep history, the sleep-timing pattern and any morning note — with a fresh random nonce per write, giving confidentiality and tamper detection together.
  • The key is generated on the device and held in the iOS Keychain, accessible only after the first unlock and marked as never leaving this device, so it is not carried into an iCloud or iTunes backup.
  • Encrypted-store files are additionally written with iOS file protection, and are excluded from device backups.
  • Named exceptions. Background photos you add, alarm bookkeeping and app-blocking rules are not in the encrypted store; Data Handling lists what each contains and why. They are still inside the iOS sandbox and covered by iOS's own file protection.
  • No plaintext personal data at rest, and no personal data in transit, because the app transmits none.

4. Application hardening

  • No third-party SDKs at all and no network requests in normal use, so there is no runtime path by which app data could reach another party.
  • Zero package dependencies, which reduces supply-chain surface to Apple's own frameworks and code we wrote.
  • The app runs inside the iOS application sandbox, so its storage is unreadable by other apps.
  • All audio is synthesised on the device. Nothing is streamed, downloaded or fetched at runtime.
  • Diagnostic and test hooks are compiled out of release builds entirely, not merely hidden.

5. Microphone and sensor safeguards

The listening modes ("Count noise" and "Auto volume") are strictly opt-in, gated behind an operating-system permission prompt, compute only a numeric loudness value locally, and never record, store, or transmit audio. No machine-learning or recognition models are used — a level meter, nothing more. The microphone is released the moment the mode is turned off or playback stops; the default mode is Off.

Morning notes are the one place audio is kept, and only if you record one. A morning note is a short recording you make deliberately, from the alarm screen, to be shown to you the next morning. It is stored on your device under the same encryption as everything else and is never uploaded. Exactly one exists at a time: recording another replaces it, and you can delete it outright at any point. If your device supports offline dictation, the note is also written out as text — that transcription runs entirely on your device through Apple's on-device speech recognition, with no network request and no third-party service involved. Where offline dictation is unavailable, Remvoll keeps the audio and does not transcribe it rather than sending your voice anywhere.

6. Payments

Payment is handled entirely by Apple. Remvoll never receives, displays or stores a card number, and there is no payment field anywhere in the app. What the app holds is Apple's signed statement of entitlement, which contains no payment information.

7. Secure development practices

  • Principle of least privilege and data minimization applied to every feature.
  • Security-relevant changes reviewed with an emphasis on injection, authentication, and data-exposure risks.
  • A dependency-light codebase to reduce the attack surface and the frequency of third-party patching.
  • Defense in depth: the iOS sandbox, file protection, Keychain storage and encryption at rest overlap, so no single control is load-bearing on its own.

8. Known limitations — the honest section

  • Encryption at rest protects the data if the device is off or locked. Anyone who can unlock your iPhone can open Remvoll and read what is in it, because there is no second password. Protect the device with a passcode, Face ID or Touch ID.
  • Because there is no account and no server backup, deleting the app or losing the device loses the data. Use Settings › Export my data for anything you want to keep.
  • Alarms depend on iOS and on the device staying powered. Do not rely on any app, this one included, as your only wake-up for something that matters.
  • No software is perfectly secure. We describe our controls candidly rather than claiming invulnerability.

9. Responsible disclosure

We welcome good-faith security research. If you believe you have found a vulnerability, please report it to security@remvoll.com with enough detail to reproduce it. Please do not test against other people's devices or accounts, do not access or modify data that is not yours, and give us a reasonable opportunity to remediate before public disclosure. There are no Remvoll servers to test against. We commit to acknowledging valid reports promptly, keeping you informed, and crediting researchers who wish to be recognized. We will not pursue legal action for good-faith research conducted in accordance with this policy.

Security contact: security@remvoll.com.
